job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Tomas Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take the train from my aunt's place in Scarborough to the university downtown, where I'm doing a master's in finance. Weekends I stock shelves at a grocery store from six in the morning. Evenings are practice exams for a professional finance certificate, with a calculator and a printed textbook, because I concentrate better on paper.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get to this point?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a finance bachelor's at the same university and passed, nothing flashy. I never got an internship, because I didn't know anyone and the applications went nowhere. I owe about 44,000 and live in my aunt's basement for 300 a month, since my parents run a small dry-cleaner and can barely cover their own rent. The master's seemed the safe route, since a bank wants a credential if you've no experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds right. Most new technology gets oversold, and in the end the work still needs people who know what they're doing. I'd say that to my aunt over dinner and not bother posting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't change anything for me. Banks around here hire maybe a handful of juniors a year and the rest go to people with connections or internships. I have neither, so I'd still be where I am: late, in debt and polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, sit the first level of the certificate in the spring, and apply to the big banks, the credit unions and the accounting firms, 50 applications. I'd keep the grocery shifts and the basement. I'd avoid any big risk, like moving cities, until I have a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Not panic, just a steady weight, like carrying a full bag of groceries all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the certificate is your plan. How sure are you that it opens a door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not sure. It helps if you pass, but plenty of people have the certificate and no job. The certificate is a ticket to a queue, not a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If hype dies down, what would you say is still hard about your situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan. 44,000 at a rate that keeps eating the payments. My parents can't help, and if the grocery store cuts hours I'm a month from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fact of life, you adapt or you don't. I'd tell classmates not to panic, but not to ignore it either. Honestly I'd say it quietly, because I don't know enough to argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. The junior work is spreadsheets, checking numbers and writing summaries, and that's exactly what the software takes. With few jobs already, the bank will say it doesn't need more juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to stop avoiding the tools, which I don't like. I'd take a short course the university offers, put the certificate on hold if I couldn't afford both, and look at jobs that need a person to meet customers, like a credit union branch. I'd also cut my phone plan and anything extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, close to afraid. Everything I planned depends on a first rung that might be sawn off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of a junior bank job do you expect software to take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checking, the reports, the matching of numbers. The human part is talking to a customer who's nervous, and nobody gives that to a newcomer, so there's nowhere to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. What would make you try one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proof that it doesn't make errors that I get blamed for. If a boss told me to use it and showed me it works, I'd try. I won't go and play with it for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know, and I'd be honest about it. I wouldn't give a speech. I'd probably say governments should slow down and give people time, but I don't expect them to listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the end of the plan. A finance degree is thinking work, the certificate is thinking work, and a bank that can have it done cheaper by software won't hire me. I'm 25 in 2028 with 44,000 of debt and no idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have a plan, honestly. I'd stay at the grocery store, which robots won't do for about three more years, and try to work more hours. I'd stop the certificate and put every spare dollar toward the loan. I'd sit with my parents and ask what we can cut in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I'd feel like I've been told the road I paid for ends in a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents, who run the dry-cleaner, that I'm sorry I took on the debt and that I'd try to work full-time at the grocery store. They'd say not to worry, and I would anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government or banks in the two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time and a cushion. Some kind of debt relief or income support if the jobs vanish, so people aren't left to drown. Banks should stop asking for experience nobody can get.

I'd say governments should slow down, but I don't expect them to listen.
think: It's the **end of the plan**, because finance and the certificate are thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so it's worth taking seriously. I'd say people should save a bit more and learn something new, and I'd say it to my own younger cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still scared, but there's room. Five years gets me through the master's, a first job if I'm lucky, and maybe a quarter of the debt. By 2031 I'd be 29 and I'd have to be somewhere useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably switch my target from big banks to something that has people in it, like a branch role or a small advisory firm. I'd put 200 a month on the loan, and I'd force myself to learn the tools at work so I don't fall behind. The certificate I'd keep, but only the first level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also tense. Five years feels like someone's put a date on my exam and I haven't studied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years allow that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the first level, because it's cheap and it shows I'm serious. I'd stop after that unless my job paid for the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still bother with the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them to get one steady job and some savings, in that order. A job with a payslip is the only thing that makes the loan manageable, and everything else follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and people overreact. I'd say it plainly at work if I had a job by then, and I'd say save while you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough that I'd probably be fine, but only if I move on something. I'm slow to change, and I know that. The risk is that I wait and then it's 2035 and I haven't built anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job and stay there, learn the tools slowly as they come to my team, and clear the loan in about eight years. Maybe add a small side thing, like doing tax returns for the neighbours. I'd build savings of three months, that's my goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, but not easy. The worry is quieter, like background noise instead of an alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you were 34 and still in this field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 34 and probably doing something with customers and numbers, like a small advisory role. If it's gone, I'd already have a second thing, so I'm not starting from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a cousin starting finance now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't take a huge loan for one narrow path, and get any work experience in the first year. And learn how people work with these tools before the job requires it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one, because I'd have no time and a loan I can't shrink. What would help is some breathing room on the debt, a guaranteed way in for new graduates, and a fair warning from the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that I'm not angry at anyone. It's like weather. I just want my family to be okay, and I'd say that to my parents even if they say they're fine.

headlineQuote: I'm not angry at anyone. It's like weather.
portrait: Tomas is a **24-year-old** finance master's student in Toronto who lives in his aunt's basement, with 44,000 in debt and no internship.
He is **centre** and pragmatic: no villains, a shrug that hides real fear.
He is **resistant** to AI and sticks to paper, so entry-level automation hits him hardest.
His mood runs from anxious to **panicked** at 2028, and stays alarmed in later worlds because he is slow to change.
He works grocery shifts, and his parents run a **dry-cleaner** and cannot help.
biggestWorry: Tomas fears **2028** most, with no time and a loan he cannot shrink.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **debt breathing room**, a guaranteed way in for graduates and fair warning.
